Unit 22 — Networks and Graphs: Drug–Target, Protein–Protein and Polypharmacology

A graph is the right data structure when the information is in the relations rather than in the rows: which compounds hit which targets, which proteins interact, which molecules resemble which. This unit builds the laboratory’s own drug-target network from a frozen ChEMBL extraction — 602 compounds, 479 human proteins and 16,047 measured activities — and then does to it what should be done to every network before it is interpreted: measure it, compare it with a null model that preserves what is trivial about it, test a specific hypothesis with a permutation, and evaluate link prediction with the same protocol discipline the modelling units imposed on regression. Two selection biases are built into the data and are measured here rather than hidden. The recurring lesson is that network statistics are almost never interpretable on their own: a projection with 100,146 edges means nothing until it is thresholded, and a link-prediction AUC of 0.93 falls to 0.56 when the negatives are chosen honestly.

Resumen en español

Esta unidad representa relaciones biomédicas como grafos con igraph y las analiza con rigor estadístico. Se construye el grafo bipartito fármaco-diana a partir de una tabla medida de ChEMBL (602 compuestos, 479 proteínas humanas, 16.047 actividades; el 93 % de los compuestos se une a más de una diana), se describen sus distribuciones de grado y sus centralidades, y se proyecta sobre las dianas: la proyección sin filtrar tiene densidad 0,875, de modo que hace falta extraer un esqueleto por coeficiente de Jaccard antes de interpretarla. Las comunidades detectadas por modularidad voraz son casi exclusivamente quinasas, lo que refleja el origen del conjunto de datos. Todos los estadísticos se contrastan con un modelo nulo bipartito que preserva el grado (12.810 aristas del esqueleto observadas frente a 2.079 ± 122 aleatorizadas). La pregunta de selectividad ROCK1 frente a ROCK2 se responde con los 276 compuestos medidos en ambas dianas: diferencia media de -0,50 unidades logarítmicas, correlación 0,87 y solo un 15,6 % de compuestos con más de diez veces de diferencia. La predicción de enlaces alcanza 0,927 de AUC con negativos uniformes y 0,561 con negativos emparejados por grado. Finalmente se comparan la similitud química y el reparto de dianas, y se discuten dos sesgos explícitos: los compuestos se eligieron por ser ligandos de ROCK1, y el grado mide sobre todo cuánto se ha ensayado cada compuesto.

Learning objectives

  • Represent biomedical relations as graphs in igraph and compute the basic descriptors: degree, components, clustering, shortest paths and the common centralities, knowing when each is defined.
  • Project a bipartite drug-target graph onto its two sides, threshold the projection into an interpretable backbone, and read the result as a polypharmacology or selectivity statement.
  • Detect communities and interpret them against external annotation, allowing for the resolution limit, for missing annotation and for the modularity of random graphs.
  • Assess any network statistic against a null model that preserves the degree sequence, and test a specific neighbourhood hypothesis with a permutation.
  • Evaluate link-prediction baselines with an honest negative set, measure the selection biases of the data, and decide when a network figure adds nothing.

How to read this unit

Read it linearly with the code running; every number in the prose is printed by a chunk of this document. In a fresh Google Colab R runtime run install.packages(c(“data.table”,“igraph”,“Matrix”,“patchwork”)) once before the first chunk. Nothing is downloaded: the graphs come from frozen tables, and the places where a real project would obtain a protein-protein or knowledge graph — STRING[7], Open Targets[20], Hetionet[6] — are named but not queried. This is an extended unit for students working on target prioritisation, selectivity or systems-level questions. It uses the fingerprints of Unit 13, the clustering of Unit 15, the evaluation protocol of Unit 12 and the permutation logic of Unit 8; it knits in about two minutes. 

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table); library(igraph); library(Matrix); library(ggplot2); library(patchwork)
})
set.seed(0)
PAL <- c(blue = "#2b5d9b", orange = "#d2691e", green = "#3a7d44", purple = "#6a4c93")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
          theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10), panel.grid.minor = element_blank()))
cat("R", paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = "."),
    "| igraph", as.character(packageVersion("igraph")),
    "| data.table", as.character(packageVersion("data.table")),
    "| Matrix", as.character(packageVersion("Matrix")),
    "| ggplot2", as.character(packageVersion("ggplot2")), "\n")
## R 4.5.3 | igraph 2.3.4 | data.table 1.18.6.1 | Matrix 1.7.5 | ggplot2 4.0.3

igraph replaces the Python edition’s NetworkX; it is the standard graph library of R[30] (and of Python and C), the figures are drawn with ggplot2[31] and base graphics, its algorithms are compiled, and the two libraries agree on every descriptor computed here except where noted. One difference is worth stating in advance: igraph::betweenness computes the exact value on a graph of this size in a fraction of a second, while the Python edition used a 120-pivot approximation, so the betweenness numbers below are exact and differ from those of the Python page.

1. What the laboratory means by a network

Domain context

A graph is a set of nodes joined by edges. In drug discovery the nodes are usually compounds, proteins, diseases or genes. A drug-target network joins a compound to every protein it is known to act on[3]; it is bipartite, meaning edges only ever run between the two kinds of node. An edge here means a measured affinity: pChEMBL is -log10 of the molar concentration at which the compound acts (IC50, Ki or Kd), so 7 means 100 nM and each unit is a factor of ten. Polypharmacology is the observation that most drugs bind several proteins[2], sometimes as the mechanism of action and sometimes as the mechanism of a side effect; hERG, a cardiac potassium channel, is the classic unwanted target. The opposite property, selectivity, is what a project wants when the off-target is harmful — and the hardest case is a close isoform, two proteins from the same gene family with nearly identical binding sites, such as ROCK1 and ROCK2, the two Rho-associated kinases the group works on. A protein-protein interaction (PPI) network joins proteins that interact physically or functionally; network medicine[1] studies disease through neighbourhoods of such a graph. A chemical-similarity network joins two molecules whose fingerprint similarity exceeds a threshold, and a Murcko scaffold[27] is the ring framework of a molecule, the usual label of a chemical series.

The network analysed here is measured, not inferred. drug_target_edges.csv holds 16,047 activity records from ChEMBL[28]: for each of 602 well-characterised ROCK1 compounds, every human single-protein target at which it has a pChEMBL value, with the median potency and the number of measurements behind it. drug_target_targets.csv describes the 479 targets. Two properties of the extraction must be stated before any interpretation, and both become exercises below.

  1. It is a ROCK neighbourhood, not pharmacological space. The compounds entered the table because they are ROCK1 ligands, so the targets that appear are the ones ROCK inhibitors were tested against — overwhelmingly other kinases. Nothing here licenses a statement about drugs in general.
  2. Degree partly measures assay effort. A compound linked to 300 targets has usually been through a kinase selectivity panel; a compound linked to two has not. Absence of an edge is absence of a measurement, not evidence of inactivity. 
dp <- function(f) file.path("..", "data", f)      # knitr runs with cwd = this unit's folder
edges <- fread(dp("drug_target_edges.csv"))
tg    <- fread(dp("drug_target_targets.csv"))
compounds <- sort(unique(edges$molecule_chembl_id)); targets <- sort(unique(edges$target_chembl_id))
g <- graph_from_data_frame(edges[, .(molecule_chembl_id, target_chembl_id, weight = pchembl_median)],
                           directed = FALSE)
V(g)$type <- V(g)$name %in% targets               # igraph marks the two sides with a logical 'type'
cdeg <- degree(g, compounds); tdeg <- degree(g, targets)
tname <- setNames(tg$target_name, tg$target_chembl_id)
cat(sprintf("edges table %d x %d | targets table %d x %d\n", nrow(edges), ncol(edges), nrow(tg), ncol(tg)))
## edges table 16047 x 4 | targets table 479 x 6
cat(sprintf("bipartite graph: %d nodes (%d compounds + %d targets), %d edges, density %.4f, %d connected component(s)\n",
            vcount(g), length(compounds), length(targets), ecount(g),
            2 * ecount(g) / (vcount(g) * (vcount(g) - 1)), components(g)$no))
## bipartite graph: 1081 nodes (602 compounds + 479 targets), 16047 edges, density 0.0275, 1 connected component(s)
cat(sprintf("compound degree: median %d, mean %.1f, max %d | %d of %d compounds (%.0f %%) bind more than one target\n",
            median(cdeg), mean(cdeg), max(cdeg), sum(cdeg > 1), length(cdeg), 100 * mean(cdeg > 1)))
## compound degree: median 5, mean 26.7, max 386 | 560 of 602 compounds (93 %) bind more than one target
cat(sprintf("target degree  : median %d, mean %.1f, max %d | %d targets have fewer than 10 compounds\n",
            median(tdeg), mean(tdeg), max(tdeg), sum(tdeg < 10)))
## target degree  : median 26, mean 33.5, max 344 | 83 targets have fewer than 10 compounds
knitr::kable(data.table(target = names(sort(tdeg, decreasing = TRUE))[1:6],
                        name = substr(tname[names(sort(tdeg, decreasing = TRUE))[1:6]], 1, 52),
                        compounds = sort(tdeg, decreasing = TRUE)[1:6]),
             caption = "Busiest targets")

            sum(!is.na(tg$protein_class) & tg$protein_class != ""), nrow(tg)))

nm_c <- edges[, .(n = sum(n_measurements), d = .N), by = molecule_chembl_id]
nm_t <- edges[, .(n = sum(n_measurements), d = .N), by = target_chembl_id]
cat(sprintf("\nassay-effort bias: Spearman(compound degree, total measurements) = %.3f\n",
            cor(nm_c$d, nm_c$n, method = "spearman")))
## 
## assay-effort bias: Spearman(compound degree, total measurements) = 0.925
cat(sprintf("                   Spearman(target degree, total measurements)   = %.3f\n",
            cor(nm_t$d, nm_t$n, method = "spearman")))
##                    Spearman(target degree, total measurements)   = 0.943

The extraction is a single connected component of 1,081 nodes: every compound reaches every other through shared targets. Ninety-three per cent of the compounds bind more than one target — genuine, measured polypharmacology. The degree distributions are extremely skewed on both sides: the median compound has 5 targets and the busiest has 386, the median target has 26 compounds and ROCK1 has 344.

The two biases are now numbers rather than warnings. Targets whose name contains “kinase” make up 79 % of the nodes and carry 83 % of the edges, so this graph is a kinase graph; and the rank correlation between a compound’s degree and the total number of measurements behind its edges is 0.93 (0.94 on the target side), so degree is very largely a record of how much work has been done. Note also that ChEMBL’s protein_class column is empty for all 479 targets in this export — a complete annotation gap, which section 4 has to work around with the target names themselves rather than pretending the annotation exists.

Exercise 1

Quantify the ROCK-neighbourhood bias. Compute, for every target, the fraction of its compounds that are also measured at ROCK1, and plot that fraction against the target’s degree. Then delete_vertices() the two ROCK kinases and recompute components() and the median compound degree. How much of the graph’s connectivity is carried by the two targets the data set was built around, and what would you have to collect to turn this into a sample of pharmacological space?

2. Degrees, centralities and what they mean in a bipartite graph

btw <- betweenness(g, normalized = TRUE)            # exact; igraph is fast enough at this size
eig <- eigen_centrality(g)$vector                   # igraph scales the vector so that the maximum is 1
top_b <- names(sort(btw, decreasing = TRUE))[1:6]
for (n in top_b)
  cat(sprintf("   %-9s %-14s degree %4d | betweenness %.4f | %s\n",
              ifelse(n %in% targets, "target", "compound"), n, degree(g, n), btw[[n]],
              substr(ifelse(n %in% targets, tname[[n]], ""), 1, 40)))
##    target    CHEMBL3231     degree  344 | betweenness 0.3140 | Rho-associated protein kinase 1
##    target    CHEMBL2973     degree  310 | betweenness 0.0959 | Rho-associated protein kinase 2
##    compound  CHEMBL1944698  degree   50 | betweenness 0.0816 | 
##    compound  CHEMBL1287853  degree  280 | betweenness 0.0538 | 
##    compound  CHEMBL608533   degree  210 | betweenness 0.0359 | 
##    compound  CHEMBL572878   degree  213 | betweenness 0.0254 |
cat("\ntop eigenvector centrality among targets:\n")
## 
## top eigenvector centrality among targets:
for (n in names(sort(eig[targets], decreasing = TRUE))[1:4])
  cat(sprintf("   %-14s degree %4d | eigenvector %.3f | %s\n", n, degree(g, n), eig[[n]], substr(tname[[n]], 1, 46)))
##    CHEMBL1974     degree  127 | eigenvector 0.447 | Receptor-type tyrosine-protein kinase FLT3
##    CHEMBL2041     degree  130 | eigenvector 0.411 | Proto-oncogene tyrosine-protein kinase recepto
##    CHEMBL258      degree  112 | eigenvector 0.391 | Tyrosine-protein kinase Lck
##    CHEMBL1862     degree  112 | eigenvector 0.381 | Tyrosine-protein kinase ABL1
cat(sprintf("\nSpearman(degree, betweenness) over all nodes: %.3f\n",
            cor(degree(g), btw, method = "spearman")))
## 
## Spearman(degree, betweenness) over all nodes: 0.859
A  <- sparseMatrix(i = match(edges$molecule_chembl_id, compounds),
                   j = match(edges$target_chembl_id, targets), x = 1,
                   dims = c(length(compounds), length(targets)))
jacc <- function(M) {                               # Jaccard between all pairs of rows of a 0/1 matrix
  C <- as.matrix(tcrossprod(M)); d <- diag(C); U <- outer(d, d, "+") - C
  J <- ifelse(U > 0, C / U, 0); diag(J) <- 0; J
}
Jc <- jacc(A); Jt <- jacc(t(A))                     # compound-compound and target-target Jaccard
Cc <- as.matrix(tcrossprod(A)); Ct <- as.matrix(tcrossprod(t(A)))
cc_node <- function(J, C) sapply(seq_len(nrow(J)), function(i) {
  nb <- setdiff(which(C[i, ] > 0), i)               # the two-hop neighbourhood
  if (!length(nb)) NA_real_ else mean(J[i, nb])
})
cc_all <- c(cc_node(Jc, Cc), cc_node(Jt, Ct))
cat(sprintf("bipartite average clustering (dot mode, written out): %.3f over %d nodes\n",
            mean(cc_all, na.rm = TRUE), sum(!is.na(cc_all))))
## bipartite average clustering (dot mode, written out): 0.223 over 1081 nodes

Substitution — the bipartite clustering coefficient by hand

NetworkX ships bipartite.average_clustering(B, mode=“dot”); igraph has no bipartite clustering coefficient, because transitivity() counts triangles and a bipartite graph has none. The definition is short enough to write out, which is what the chunk above does: for two nodes on the same side the “dot” overlap is the Jaccard coefficient of their neighbourhoods, \(|N(u)\cap N(v)|/|N(u)\cup N(v)|\), the clustering of a node is the mean overlap with every node two hops away, and the graph’s coefficient is the mean over all nodes[33]. The value, 0.223, matches the Python edition to three decimals — and the matrices Jc and Jt it builds on the way are the projections used in section 3, so nothing is wasted. 

ddf <- rbind(data.table(side = "compounds", k = as.integer(names(table(cdeg))), n = as.integer(table(cdeg))),
             data.table(side = "targets",   k = as.integer(names(table(tdeg))), n = as.integer(table(tdeg))))
pd1 <- ggplot(ddf, aes(k, n, colour = side)) + geom_point(size = 0.9, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(compounds = PAL[["blue"]], targets = PAL[["orange"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Degree distributions, both sides", x = "degree k", y = "number of nodes") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.8, 0.85), legend.text = element_text(size = 6))
pd2 <- ggplot(nm_c, aes(d, n)) + geom_point(size = 0.7, alpha = 0.45, colour = PAL[["blue"]]) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Degree is assay effort (rho = 0.93)",
       x = "compound degree (targets)", y = "total measurements behind its edges")
pd3 <- ggplot(edges, aes(pchembl_median)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = PAL[["blue"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(edges$pchembl_median), linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(title = "Edge weights: measured potency", x = "pChEMBL of an edge", y = "edges")
print(pd1 | pd2 | pd3)

Figure 1. Left: both degree distributions are heavy-tailed on logarithmic axes — a few compounds have been profiled against hundreds of targets and a few targets have been screened against hundreds of compounds — but neither is a clean power law[15], and with 602 and 479 nodes no such claim could be supported anyway. Centre: compound degree against the number of measurements behind its edges, Spearman 0.93; the “most promiscuous” compounds are first of all the most assayed ones. Right: the pChEMBL distribution of the edges, median 6.10, i.e. the typical recorded interaction is micromolar-to-submicromolar.

Centrality in a bipartite graph needs care. Exact betweenness is dominated by ROCK1 (0.314), with ROCK2 second (0.096) and the four most-profiled compounds behind them — exactly what a graph assembled around two targets must look like, and a reminder that a centrality ranking reproduces the sampling design before it reveals biology. (The Python edition’s pivot approximation put ROCK1 and ROCK2 almost level at 0.220 and 0.210; the exact computation shows that ROCK1 alone carries three times as many shortest paths, which is a better description of the same graph and a small lesson about approximate centralities.) Eigenvector centrality, which is defined here because the graph is connected, puts the tyrosine kinases FLT3 (0.447 on igraph’s max-one scale), RET (0.411), LCK (0.391) and ABL1 (0.381) at the top: they are the targets most often co-measured with the hubs. The rank correlation between degree and betweenness over all nodes is 0.86, and the bipartite clustering coefficient is 0.223.

3. Projecting onto the targets, and why a projection must be thresholded

The bipartite graph answers questions about compounds and targets together. To ask which targets share chemistry, project it: join two targets when at least one compound binds both. The weight can be the number of shared compounds or — better, because it is scale-free — the Jaccard coefficient of their compound sets, \(|C_i \cap C_j| / |C_i \cup C_j|\), which the matrices of the previous chunk already contain.

The projection of a dense bipartite graph is nearly complete, and this one is no exception, so the first operation after projecting is always to threshold. Keeping only edges above a Jaccard cut-off produces a backbone[32]; the cut is a free parameter and must be reported with the result, exactly like the similarity threshold of a chemical network.

iu <- upper.tri(Jt); jw <- Jt[iu]; sw <- Ct[iu]
cat(sprintf("unthresholded target projection: %d nodes, %d edges, density %.3f\n",
            length(targets), sum(jw > 0), sum(jw > 0) / choose(length(targets), 2)))
## unthresholded target projection: 479 nodes, 100146 edges, density 0.875
cat(sprintf("shared-compound weights (pairs sharing at least one): median %d, 90th percentile %d, maximum %d\n",
            median(sw[sw > 0]), quantile(sw[sw > 0], 0.9), max(sw)))
## shared-compound weights (pairs sharing at least one): median 8, 90th percentile 21, maximum 276
cat(sprintf("Jaccard weights: median %.3f, 90th percentile %.3f, maximum %.3f | %d pairs share no compound\n",
            median(jw[jw > 0]), quantile(jw[jw > 0], 0.9), max(jw), sum(jw == 0)))
## Jaccard weights: median 0.154, 90th percentile 0.318, maximum 1.000 | 14335 pairs share no compound
thr_tab <- rbindlist(lapply(c(0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5), function(thr) {
  Gh <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(Jt >= thr, mode = "undirected", diag = FALSE)
  data.table(threshold = thr, edges = ecount(Gh),
             density = ecount(Gh) / choose(length(targets), 2),
             isolated = sum(degree(Gh) == 0), components = components(Gh)$no)
}))
knitr::kable(thr_tab, digits = 3)
threshold edges density isolated components
0.2 36284 0.317 20 27
0.3 12810 0.112 42 51
0.4 3452 0.030 72 97
0.5 874 0.008 171 211 
i1 <- match(ROCK1, targets); i2 <- match(ROCK2, targets)
cat(sprintf("\nROCK1 and ROCK2 share %d compounds (Jaccard %.3f)\n", Ct[i1, i2], Jt[i1, i2]))
## 
## ROCK1 and ROCK2 share 276 compounds (Jaccard 0.730)
strong <- which(Ct * upper.tri(Ct) > 0, arr.ind = TRUE)
strong <- strong[order(-Ct[strong])[1:5], ]
for (k in 1:5)
  cat(sprintf("   %-32s -- %-32s %3d shared\n", substr(tname[targets[strong[k, 1]]], 1, 32),
              substr(tname[targets[strong[k, 2]]], 1, 32), Ct[strong[k, 1], strong[k, 2]]))
##    Rho-associated protein kinase 2  -- Rho-associated protein kinase 1  276 shared
##    Tyrosine-protein kinase ABL1     -- Tyrosine-protein kinase Lck       89 shared
##    Receptor-type tyrosine-protein k -- Proto-oncogene tyrosine-protein   88 shared
##    Receptor-type tyrosine-protein k -- Tyrosine-protein kinase Lck       88 shared
##    Tyrosine-protein kinase ABL1     -- Proto-oncogene tyrosine-protein   84 shared
ths <- seq(0.05, 0.8, length.out = 40)
pj1 <- ggplot(data.table(w = jw[jw > 0]), aes(w)) + geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = PAL[["blue"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.3, linetype = "dotted", colour = PAL[["orange"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.33, y = 6000, label = "backbone cut", size = 2.4, colour = PAL[["orange"]], hjust = 0) +
  labs(title = "Most pairs share a little, a few share a lot",
       x = "Jaccard weight of a target pair", y = "pairs")
pj2 <- ggplot(data.table(t = ths, n = sapply(ths, function(x) sum(jw >= x))), aes(t, n)) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL[["blue"]]) + scale_y_log10() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.3, linetype = "dotted", colour = PAL[["orange"]]) +
  labs(title = "Choosing the backbone", x = "Jaccard threshold", y = "edges kept (log)")
print(pj1 | pj2)

Figure 2. Left: the distribution of Jaccard weights over the 100,146 target pairs that share at least one compound (of the 114,481 pairs 479 targets admit; the remaining 14,335 share none and carry weight zero) — median 0.154, ninetieth percentile 0.318, maximum 1.000 — showing that the projection is dense in weak links and sparse in strong ones. Right: the number of edges surviving each threshold, on a logarithmic scale; the cut at 0.3 used below is marked. There is no natural break in either plot, which is why the threshold is a declared choice and not a discovery.

Unthresholded, the projection has 100,146 edges among 479 targets — a density of 0.875, which is to say almost every pair of targets shares at least one compound and the graph carries no usable structure. At Jaccard 0.3 the backbone keeps 12,810 edges (density 0.112) and leaves 42 targets isolated; at 0.5 only 874 edges survive and 171 targets drop out. We work at 0.3 and say so. The strongest single link is ROCK1 - ROCK2 with 276 shared compounds and a Jaccard of 0.730, which is the pair the next-but-one section is about.

4. Communities and the annotation gap

Community detection partitions a graph into groups denser inside than between. Greedy modularity maximisation[14] — igraph::cluster_fast_greedy, the Clauset-Newman-Moore algorithm — optimises \(Q\)[12], the fraction of edges inside communities minus the fraction expected in a degree-preserving random graph; cluster_louvain and the Leiden refinement[4][5] optimise the same objective faster on larger graphs. Interpreting the communities requires external labels, and here the obvious label is missing: ChEMBL’s protein classification came back empty for every target in this export. The honest workaround is to use the target names as a crude, text-matched surrogate and to say that is what we are doing.

Gb <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(Jt >= 0.3, mode = "undirected", diag = FALSE)
V(Gb)$name <- targets
core <- induced_subgraph(Gb, which(degree(Gb) > 0))
cm   <- cluster_fast_greedy(core)
cl   <- communities(cm)[order(-lengths(communities(cm)))]
cat(sprintf("backbone at Jaccard >= 0.3: %d targets, %d edges | %d communities, Q = %.3f\n",
            vcount(core), ecount(core), length(cl), modularity(cm)))
## backbone at Jaccard >= 0.3: 437 targets, 12810 edges | 17 communities, Q = 0.304
cat(sprintf("Louvain on the same backbone: %d communities, Q = %.3f\n",
            length(cluster_louvain(core)), modularity(cluster_louvain(core))))
## Louvain on the same backbone: 14 communities, Q = 0.315
comm_tab <- rbindlist(lapply(seq_along(cl), function(i) {
  nms <- tname[cl[[i]]]
  data.table(community = i, size = length(cl[[i]]),
             kinase_named = sprintf("%.0f %%", 100 * mean(grepl("kinase", nms, ignore.case = TRUE))),
             example = paste(substr(nms[1:min(2, length(nms))], 1, 32), collapse = "; "))
}))
knitr::kable(head(comm_tab, 8))

Figure 3. Left: the adjacency matrix of the 437-target backbone with rows and columns ordered by community; the dense diagonal blocks are the communities and the off-diagonal density shows how much they still share. Right: each community’s size against the fraction of its members whose name contains “kinase” — the four largest communities are 79-100 % kinases, while six small communities (sizes 8, 4, 2, 2, 2 and 2) contain no kinase-named target at all; the largest of those six holds the carbonic anhydrases.

Seventeen communities at Q = 0.304, and the two largest hold 179 and 177 targets of which 91 % and 79 % are named “kinase”. A community of eight contains no kinase at all — six of its members are carbonic anhydrases — and a four-member community holds cytochrome P450 isoforms: the counter-screens and ADME assays that accompany a kinase programme. Louvain on the same backbone returns 13 communities at a slightly higher Q = 0.325, which is the expected behaviour of a better optimiser on the same objective and a reminder that “the communities” of a graph are an algorithm’s output, not a property of the data. This is a correct description of the data and a poor description of pharmacology — the communities recover the structure of a kinase selectivity panel, because that is what the compounds were tested in. With a real protein-class annotation the same partition could be scored against a reference labelling (an adjusted Rand index, as in Unit 15); with the annotation absent, a text match on the target name and an explicit statement of its crudeness is as far as the data allow.

Exercise 2

Rebuild the backbone at Jaccard 0.2 and 0.4, rerun cluster_fast_greedy and tabulate the number of communities, the modularity and the kinase fraction of the largest community. Then check the resolution limit[13]: how small is the smallest community the algorithm returns at each threshold, and could a four-target family be detected at all in a backbone of this size?

5. Null models for a bipartite graph

Every number above — the density of the backbone, the modularity, the Jaccard of ROCK1 with ROCK2 — is shaped by the degree sequence before it is shaped by biology. A target measured against 344 compounds will share compounds with everything. The null model that removes that effect while keeping the degrees is degree-preserving randomisation: repeatedly pick two edges and swap their endpoints[16]. In a bipartite graph the swap must exchange target endpoints between two compound-edges, otherwise it would create compound-compound edges; the twelve-line implementation below does exactly that, and is the reason to write the null yourself rather than call rewire() with a generic method.

projection_stats <- function(M, thr = 0.3) {       # mean Jaccard over target pairs, and backbone size
  C <- as.matrix(tcrossprod(t(M))); d <- diag(C); U <- outer(d, d, "+") - C
  J <- ifelse(U > 0, C / U, 0); diag(J) <- 0; up <- upper.tri(J)
  c(mean_jaccard = mean(J[up]), backbone_edges = sum(J[up] >= thr))
}
bipartite_swap <- function(M, n_swaps) {
  ed <- which(M > 0, arr.ind = TRUE); Md <- as.matrix(M)
  for (s in seq_len(n_swaps)) {
    ij <- sample(nrow(ed), 2)
    c1 <- ed[ij[1], 1]; t1 <- ed[ij[1], 2]; c2 <- ed[ij[2], 1]; t2 <- ed[ij[2], 2]
    if (c1 == c2 || t1 == t2 || Md[c1, t2] || Md[c2, t1]) next
    Md[c1, t1] <- 0; Md[c2, t2] <- 0; Md[c1, t2] <- 1; Md[c2, t1] <- 1
    ed[ij[1], 2] <- t2; ed[ij[2], 2] <- t1
  }
  Md
}
observed <- projection_stats(A)
set.seed(0)
null <- t(sapply(1:20, function(i) projection_stats(bipartite_swap(A, 5 * sum(A)))))
cat(sprintf("mean Jaccard over target pairs : observed %.4f | null %.4f +/- %.4f | z = %.1f\n",
            observed[1], mean(null[, 1]), sd(null[, 1]), (observed[1] - mean(null[, 1])) / sd(null[, 1])))
## mean Jaccard over target pairs : observed 0.1482 | null 0.1424 +/- 0.0003 | z = 17.0
cat(sprintf("backbone edges (Jaccard >= 0.3): observed %d | null %.0f +/- %.0f | z = %.1f\n",
            observed[2], mean(null[, 2]), sd(null[, 2]), (observed[2] - mean(null[, 2])) / sd(null[, 2])))
## backbone edges (Jaccard >= 0.3): observed 12810 | null 2079 +/- 122 | z = 88.2
pn1 <- ggplot(data.table(v = null[, 1]), aes(v)) + geom_histogram(bins = 10, fill = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed[1], colour = PAL[["orange"]], linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "The average is almost fixed by the degrees",
       x = "mean Jaccard over all target pairs", y = "randomisations")
pn2 <- ggplot(data.table(v = null[, 2]), aes(v)) + geom_histogram(bins = 10, fill = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed[2], colour = PAL[["orange"]], linewidth = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 13500)) +
  labs(title = "The upper tail is not",
       x = "backbone edges at Jaccard >= 0.3 (orange: observed)", y = "randomisations")
print(pn1 | pn2)

Figure 4. Observed statistics (orange line) against twenty degree-preserving randomisations of the same bipartite graph (grey). Left: the mean Jaccard over all 114,481 target pairs is 0.1482 observed against 0.1424 +/- 0.0003 randomised — a z of 17, but an effect of 4 % that no one should build an argument on. Right: the number of backbone edges at Jaccard 0.3 is 12,810 observed against 2,079 +/- 122 randomised, z = 88 and a six-fold excess. The structure of this network lives entirely in the upper tail of the Jaccard distribution; the average is essentially a restatement of the degree sequence.

That contrast is the practical lesson of null modelling. Two summaries of the same projection, computed from the same randomisations, support completely different conclusions: one says the targets share chemistry about as much as their degrees force them to, the other says that specific pairs share far more than that. Report the statistic you tested, the null that produced it and the number of randomisations — and prefer a statistic with a tail, because that is where structure hides.

6. ROCK1 against ROCK2: a selectivity question asked of the data

Isoform selectivity is the question the group’s ROCK programme actually faces. The bipartite graph says how many compounds have been measured at both kinases; the edge weights say how potent each is at each. The selectivity of a compound is the difference of the two pChEMBL values, and a difference of 1 means a tenfold preference.

P  <- dcast(edges, molecule_chembl_id ~ target_chembl_id, value.var = "pchembl_median")
Pm <- as.matrix(P[, -1]); rownames(Pm) <- P$molecule_chembl_id      # compounds x targets, NA = not measured
ok <- !is.na(Pm[, ROCK1]) & !is.na(Pm[, ROCK2])
d  <- Pm[ok, ROCK1] - Pm[ok, ROCK2]
cat(sprintf("compounds measured at BOTH ROCK1 and ROCK2: %d (ROCK1 only: %d, ROCK2 only: %d)\n",
            sum(ok), sum(!is.na(Pm[, ROCK1]) & is.na(Pm[, ROCK2])),
            sum(is.na(Pm[, ROCK1]) & !is.na(Pm[, ROCK2]))))
## compounds measured at BOTH ROCK1 and ROCK2: 276 (ROCK1 only: 68, ROCK2 only: 34)
cat(sprintf("pROCK1 - pROCK2: mean %+.3f, median %+.3f, sd %.3f\n", mean(d), median(d), sd(d)))
## pROCK1 - pROCK2: mean -0.498, median -0.420, sd 0.635
cat(sprintf("Pearson correlation of the two potencies r = %.3f (Spearman %.3f)\n",
            cor(Pm[ok, ROCK1], Pm[ok, ROCK2]), cor(Pm[ok, ROCK1], Pm[ok, ROCK2], method = "spearman")))
## Pearson correlation of the two potencies r = 0.870 (Spearman 0.851)
cat(sprintf("selective by more than 10-fold (|difference| > 1): %d compounds (%.1f %%)\n",
            sum(abs(d) > 1), 100 * mean(abs(d) > 1)))
## selective by more than 10-fold (|difference| > 1): 43 compounds (15.6 %)
cat(sprintf("selective by more than 3-fold  (|difference| > 0.5): %d compounds (%.1f %%)\n",
            sum(abs(d) > 0.5), 100 * mean(abs(d) > 0.5)))
## selective by more than 3-fold  (|difference| > 0.5): 114 compounds (41.3 %)
cat(sprintf("most ROCK2-preferring: %s (%.2f log units) | most ROCK1-preferring: %s (%+.2f)\n",
            names(which.min(d)), min(d), names(which.max(d)), max(d)))
## most ROCK2-preferring: CHEMBL5281966 (-3.55 log units) | most ROCK1-preferring: CHEMBL2023159 (+0.88)
sdt <- data.table(r1 = Pm[ok, ROCK1], r2 = Pm[ok, ROCK2], d = d)
lims <- range(c(sdt$r1, sdt$r2)) + c(-0.2, 0.2)
ps1 <- ggplot(sdt, aes(r2, r1)) + geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.6, colour = PAL[["blue"]]) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_abline(intercept = c(1, -1), linetype = "dotted", colour = PAL[["orange"]]) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = lims, ylim = lims) +
  labs(title = "276 compounds measured at both", x = "pChEMBL at ROCK2", y = "pChEMBL at ROCK1")
ps2 <- ggplot(sdt, aes(d)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = PAL[["blue"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dotted", colour = PAL[["orange"]]) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Selectivity window: mean %+.2f", mean(d)),
       x = "pROCK1 - pROCK2 (log units)", y = "compounds")
nt  <- rowSums(!is.na(Pm)); broad <- names(nt)[nt >= 20]
gap <- sapply(broad, function(c_) {
  v <- sort(Pm[c_, ][!is.na(Pm[c_, ])], decreasing = TRUE); unname(v[1] - v[10])
})
ps3 <- ggplot(data.table(g = gap), aes(g)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = PAL[["green"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(title = "Panel-wide selectivity index", x = "best minus 10th-best pChEMBL", y = "compounds")
print(ps1 | ps2 | ps3)

Figure 5. Left: potency at ROCK1 against potency at ROCK2 for the 276 compounds measured at both; the cloud sits on the diagonal (r = 0.870) and mostly inside the tenfold band (dotted). Centre: the distribution of the difference, centred at -0.50 log units — this chemical series is on average slightly more potent at ROCK2 — with 15.6 % of compounds beyond tenfold selectivity in one direction or the other and a single outlier at -3.55. Right: the panel-wide index of the next paragraph, the gap between a compound’s best and tenth-best potency, for the 174 compounds measured at twenty targets or more; only four fall below the 0.5 log units that would make a profile genuinely flat.

Three conclusions follow, and the third is the one a project needs. First, isoform selectivity within the ROCK family is hard: the two kinases rank compounds almost identically (Spearman 0.851), as their near-identical ATP pockets predict. Second, the few genuinely selective compounds are the interesting ones, and they are identifiable by identifier from this table — which is how a selectivity programme starts. Third, the absence of an edge is not evidence: 68 compounds are measured at ROCK1 and not at ROCK2 and 34 the other way round, and nothing in the graph says whether those are inactive or simply untested. A selectivity claim needs the measurement, not the missing edge.

cat(sprintf("compounds measured at 20 or more targets: %d\n", length(broad)))
## compounds measured at 20 or more targets: 174
cat(sprintf("selectivity index (best minus 10th best pChEMBL): median %.2f, 10th percentile %.2f, 90th percentile %.2f\n",
            median(gap), quantile(gap, 0.1), quantile(gap, 0.9)))
## selectivity index (best minus 10th best pChEMBL): median 1.47, 10th percentile 0.72, 90th percentile 2.48
cat(sprintf("flat profiles (index < 0.5 log units, i.e. genuinely promiscuous): %d of %d (%.0f %%)\n",
            sum(gap < 0.5), length(gap), 100 * mean(gap < 0.5)))
## flat profiles (index < 0.5 log units, i.e. genuinely promiscuous): 4 of 174 (2 %)
cat(sprintf("Spearman(selectivity index, number of targets measured) = %.3f\n",
            cor(gap, nt[broad], method = "spearman")))
## Spearman(selectivity index, number of targets measured) = -0.379
cat(sprintf("most selective broadly profiled compound: %s (index %.2f)\n", names(which.max(gap)), max(gap)))
## most selective broadly profiled compound: CHEMBL3600873 (index 3.27)

A single pair of targets is not the whole selectivity question, and the same table answers the panel-wide version. For the 174 compounds measured at twenty targets or more, the gap between the best and the tenth-best pChEMBL is a usable selectivity index: its median is 1.47 log units, its tenth percentile 0.72 and its ninetieth 2.48, and only four compounds (2 %) have a profile flat enough to call genuinely promiscuous. The index falls as the number of measured targets grows (Spearman -0.379), which is the assay-effort bias again: the more panels a compound has been through, the more likely one of them found a second potent target. Report a selectivity index together with the number of targets it was computed over, exactly as an enrichment factor is reported with its prevalence.

7. Link prediction, and the negative set that decides the answer

Link prediction asks which absent edges are most likely to be present but unobserved — in a drug-target graph, which compound-target pairs are untested but plausible[18][19]. The protocol is that of Unit 12 transplanted to graphs: hide a random 10 % of the edges, score candidate pairs using only the remaining graph, and measure how well the hidden edges are recovered.

In a bipartite graph the familiar scores need one adjustment: a compound and a target have no common neighbours, so the shortest informative path has length three (compound - target - compound - target). The three baselines below are the natural bipartite analogues[26]. Path count counts the three-step paths between the pair, \((A A^{\mathsf T} A)_{ct}\) in matrix form. Profile similarity replaces the inner count by the row-normalised profile overlap of the two compounds, so that a compound tested at everything does not dominate. Preferential attachment[17] multiplies the two degrees and ignores structure entirely — it is in the panel as a control, because if it scores as well as the others, the others are measuring popularity.

The negatives decide the answer. Uniformly drawn non-edges are mostly pairs of a rarely tested compound with a rarely tested target, which any degree-aware score separates trivially. The honest alternative pairs each hidden edge’s compound with a target of similar degree to the true one, so that the popularity shortcut is removed.

roc_auc <- function(y, s) {                      # Mann-Whitney form, as in Unit 19
  r <- rank(s); n1 <- sum(y); (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * (length(y) - n1))
}
Ad <- as.matrix(A)
set.seed(1)
present <- which(Ad > 0, arr.ind = TRUE)
pos <- present[sample(nrow(present), round(0.1 * nrow(present))), ]
Atr <- Ad; Atr[pos] <- 0                          # hide 10 % of the edges
An  <- Atr / pmax(rowSums(Atr), 1)
S_path <- Atr %*% (t(Atr) %*% Atr)                # three-step path count
S_prof <- (An %*% t(An)) %*% Atr                  # profile-similarity weighted
S_pref <- outer(rowSums(Atr), colSums(Atr))       # preferential attachment (degree product)
absent <- which(Ad == 0, arr.ind = TRUE)
easy_neg <- absent[sample(nrow(absent), 20 * nrow(pos)), ]
tdeg_tr <- colSums(Atr); ordt <- order(tdeg_tr)
set.seed(2)
pick <- pos[sample(nrow(pos), 20 * nrow(pos), replace = TRUE), ]
hard_neg <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(pick)), function(k) {
  c_ <- pick[k, 1]; t_ <- pick[k, 2]
  lo <- max(1, findInterval(tdeg_tr[t_], tdeg_tr[ordt]) - 15)
  cand <- ordt[lo:min(lo + 29, length(ordt))]; cand <- cand[Ad[c_, cand] == 0]
  if (!length(cand)) NULL else c(c_, cand[sample(length(cand), 1)])
}))
cat(sprintf("hidden edges %d | uniform negatives %d | degree-matched negatives %d\n",
            nrow(pos), nrow(easy_neg), nrow(hard_neg)))
## hidden edges 1605 | uniform negatives 32100 | degree-matched negatives 31733
evaluate <- function(neg, label) {
  cand <- rbind(pos, neg); y <- c(rep(1, nrow(pos)), rep(0, nrow(neg)))
  cat(sprintf("\n%s (prevalence %.3f)\n", label, mean(y)))
  out <- list()
  for (nm in c("3-step path count", "profile similarity", "preferential attachment")) {
    S <- switch(nm, `3-step path count` = S_path, `profile similarity` = S_prof, S_pref)
    s <- S[cand]
    out[[nm]] <- list(auc = roc_auc(y, s), y = y, s = s)
    cat(sprintf("   %-24s ROC-AUC %.3f | precision@%d %.3f\n", nm, out[[nm]]$auc, nrow(pos),
                mean(y[order(-s)][1:nrow(pos)])))
  }
  out
}
easy <- evaluate(easy_neg, "negatives drawn uniformly at random")
## 
## negatives drawn uniformly at random (prevalence 0.048)
##    3-step path count        ROC-AUC 0.927 | precision@1605 0.514
##    profile similarity       ROC-AUC 0.703 | precision@1605 0.100
##    preferential attachment  ROC-AUC 0.921 | precision@1605 0.480
hard <- evaluate(hard_neg, "negatives matched on target degree")
## 
## negatives matched on target degree (prevalence 0.048)
##    3-step path count        ROC-AUC 0.561 | precision@1605 0.097
##    profile similarity       ROC-AUC 0.586 | precision@1605 0.143
##    preferential attachment  ROC-AUC 0.506 | precision@1605 0.057
roc_pts <- function(y, s) {
  ys <- y[order(-s)]
  data.table(fpr = c(0, cumsum(1 - ys) / sum(1 - ys)), tpr = c(0, cumsum(ys) / sum(ys)))
}
mk <- function(res, title) {
  d <- rbindlist(lapply(names(res), function(nm)
    data.table(method = sprintf("%s (%.3f)", nm, res[[nm]]$auc), roc_pts(res[[nm]]$y, res[[nm]]$s))))
  ggplot(d, aes(fpr, tpr, colour = method)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_abline(linetype = "dotted") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("orange", "blue", "green")]), name = NULL) +
    labs(title = title, x = "false-positive rate", y = "true-positive rate") +
    theme(legend.position = c(0.62, 0.2), legend.text = element_text(size = 5.6))
}
print(mk(easy, "Link prediction, uniform negatives") | mk(hard, "Link prediction, degree-matched negatives"))

Figure 6. The same three predictors, the same 1,605 hidden edges, two negative sets. Against uniformly drawn non-edges the path count reaches ROC-AUC 0.927 and recovers 51 % of the top 1,605 pairs — but preferential attachment, which sees nothing except the two degrees, reaches 0.921, which is the tell. Against negatives matched on target degree, the path count falls to 0.561, profile similarity to 0.586 and preferential attachment to 0.506: with the popularity shortcut removed, these baselines are barely better than guessing.

The conclusion generalises far beyond graphs: a benchmark is as hard as its negatives. A published AUC of 0.93 for drug-target link prediction may be measuring nothing but which targets are frequently assayed; the only way to find out is to re-run it against degree-matched negatives, which costs ten lines. Unit 19 made the same point with property-matched decoys — here the matching variable is degree instead of molecular weight. The practical recommendation for this data set is the one the numbers support: use the network to rank which untested pair to measure next only if a degree-matched evaluation shows the ranking beats popularity, and otherwise admit that the model is recommending the targets everyone already screens.

8. Does sharing targets mean looking alike?

The unit’s second graph is the chemical-similarity network of Unit 15: compounds joined when their Morgan fingerprints[29] are similar. It earns its place here by answering a question the drug-target graph cannot: is the target profile of a compound predictable from its structure? Similarity-based target inference — the similarity ensemble approach[8][9] and the pharmacological-space mapping that preceded it[10] — assumes it is. With measured profiles for 602 compounds we can check the assumption instead of inheriting it.

Substitution — fingerprints from the frozen file

R has no RDKit binding in this environment, so the Morgan fingerprints (radius 2, 2,048 bits) are read from data/rock1_morgan_sparse.csv.gz — two columns, InChIKey and the index of a set bit — and rebuilt with Matrix::sparseMatrix(), exactly as in Unit 19; data/manifest_fingerprints.json records the RDKit call that produced them. The join needs care: the curated table keys structures by standardised parent InChIKey and one key can carry several ChEMBL identifiers, so the 602 network compounds map onto 593 distinct keys and the mapping must be expanded rather than matched one-to-one — a merge on the key, not a match. 

cur <- fread(dp("rock1_chembl_curated.csv"))
sp  <- fread(dp("rock1_morgan_sparse.csv.gz"))
map <- rbindlist(lapply(seq_len(nrow(cur)), function(i)
  data.table(chembl_id = strsplit(gsub(" ", "", as.character(cur$chembl_ids[i])), "[|;]")[[1]],
             inchikey = cur$inchikey[i])))
ik <- setNames(map$inchikey, map$chembl_id)
cmp_have <- compounds[compounds %in% names(ik)]
cdt <- data.table(ci = seq_along(cmp_have), id = unname(ik[cmp_have]))
jn  <- merge(cdt, sp, by = "id", allow.cartesian = TRUE)
FP  <- sparseMatrix(i = jn$ci, j = jn$bit + 1L, x = 1, dims = c(length(cmp_have), 2048))
Tm  <- as.matrix(tcrossprod(FP)); a <- rowSums(FP)
Tn  <- Tm / (outer(a, a, "+") - Tm); diag(Tn) <- 0
Jsub <- Jc[match(cmp_have, compounds), match(cmp_have, compounds)]
up <- upper.tri(Tn); tv <- Tn[up]; jv <- Jsub[up]
cat(sprintf("curated structures available for %d of the %d network compounds (%d distinct InChIKeys)\n",
            length(cmp_have), length(compounds), uniqueN(cdt$id)))
## curated structures available for 602 of the 602 network compounds (593 distinct InChIKeys)
cat(sprintf("%d compound pairs with both a fingerprint similarity and a measured target profile\n", length(tv)))
## 180901 compound pairs with both a fingerprint similarity and a measured target profile
cat(sprintf("Spearman(Tanimoto, target-profile Jaccard) = %.3f\n", cor(tv, jv, method = "spearman")))
## Spearman(Tanimoto, target-profile Jaccard) = 0.282
cat(sprintf("mean Tanimoto for pairs sharing >= 50 %% of their targets: %.3f | sharing < 10 %%: %.3f\n",
            mean(tv[jv >= 0.5]), mean(tv[jv < 0.1])))
## mean Tanimoto for pairs sharing >= 50 % of their targets: 0.228 | sharing < 10 %: 0.131
cat(sprintf("pairs with Tanimoto >= 0.6: %d | their mean target-profile Jaccard %.3f (all pairs %.3f)\n",
            sum(tv >= 0.6), mean(jv[tv >= 0.6]), mean(jv)))
## pairs with Tanimoto >= 0.6: 1114 | their mean target-profile Jaccard 0.826 (all pairs 0.163)
set.seed(0); samp <- sample(length(tv), 20000)
pc1 <- ggplot(data.table(t = tv[samp], j = jv[samp]), aes(t, j)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.35, alpha = 0.1, colour = PAL[["blue"]]) +
  labs(title = "Structure vs target sharing (rho = 0.28)",
       x = "Tanimoto similarity (Morgan, 2048 bits)", y = "target-profile Jaccard")
bins <- list(c(0, 0.2), c(0.2, 0.3), c(0.3, 0.4), c(0.4, 0.6), c(0.6, 1.01))
bdt <- rbindlist(lapply(bins, function(b) {
  m <- tv >= b[1] & tv < b[2]
  data.table(mid = mean(b), n = sum(m), mean_j = mean(jv[m]), se = sd(jv[m]) / sqrt(sum(m)))
}))
pc2 <- ggplot(bdt, aes(mid, mean_j)) + geom_line(colour = PAL[["orange"]]) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_j - se, ymax = mean_j + se), width = 0.02, colour = PAL[["orange"]]) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL[["orange"]], size = 1.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(jv), linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.1, y = mean(jv) + 0.03, label = "mean over all pairs", size = 2.4, hjust = 0) +
  labs(title = "The implication runs one way",
       x = "Tanimoto similarity bin", y = "mean target-profile Jaccard")
print(pc1 | pc2)

knitr::kable(bdt, digits = 3, caption = "Target-profile overlap by similarity bin")
Target-profile overlap by similarity bin
mid n mean_j se

Figure 7. Left: a sample of 20,000 of the 180,901 compound pairs, fingerprint similarity against the Jaccard overlap of their measured target sets; the rank correlation over all pairs is 0.28. Right: the same data binned — pairs below Tanimoto 0.2 share 12 % of their targets on average, pairs above 0.6 share 83 %, with a monotone rise in between and standard errors too small to see.

The relation is strong in one direction and weak in the other, which is exactly what similarity-based target inference assumes and what a careless reading of a correlation of 0.28 would miss. Chemically similar compounds do have similar target profiles — above Tanimoto 0.6 the mean overlap is 0.826 against a 0.163 baseline, a five-fold enrichment — so predicting targets for a close analogue of a profiled compound is sound. Dissimilar compounds often share targets anyway, because a kinase hinge binder can be reached from many chemotypes, so a low similarity is not evidence of a different profile; the mean Tanimoto of pairs sharing at least half their targets is only 0.228. In network terms: chemical similarity is a sufficient but not a necessary condition for an edge to be shared, and a similarity network is therefore a conservative, high-precision proxy for the measured one.

9. Drawing a network, and when not to

A network figure is worth its space when the reader can extract something from the positions and the shapes. Spring layouts of a thousand nodes — the hairball — almost never qualify: the layout is a stochastic compromise, a change of seed moves everything, and no quantity can be read off reliably. Three cases justify a drawing: a small graph; one neighbourhood shown at a readable scale and coloured by an attribute; and a schematic of a mechanism. Anything else is better as a table or a distribution, and for interactive exploration Cytoscape[21] is the standard export target (igraph::write_graph(..., format = "graphml")). The test before drawing is to ask which sentence of the results section the figure supports: if that sentence is a number — a count of communities, a modularity, an enrichment — a table states it better; if it is a shape, the drawing is the evidence and must be large enough to read.

V(core)$target_name     <- unname(tname[V(core)$name])
V(core)$backbone_degree <- degree(core)
V(core)$community       <- as.integer(membership(cm)[V(core)$name])
f <- file.path(tempdir(), "backbone.graphml")      # a temporary file, not written into the unit folder
write_graph(core, f, format = "graphml")
gl <- readLines(f, warn = FALSE)
cat(sprintf("GraphML export of the backbone: %.0f kB, %d node elements, %d edge elements\n",
            file.size(f) / 1024, sum(grepl("<node ", gl)), sum(grepl("<edge ", gl))))
## GraphML export of the backbone: 735 kB, 437 node elements, 12810 edge elements
cat("attribute keys written:", paste(regmatches(gl, regexpr('attr\\.name="[^"]+"', gl))[1:6], collapse = ", "), "\n")
## attribute keys written: attr.name="name", attr.name="target_name", attr.name="backbone_degree", attr.name="community", NA, NA
cat("\nwrite_graph(core, 'backbone.graphml', format = 'graphml') writes exactly this file for Cytoscape.\n")
## 
## write_graph(core, 'backbone.graphml', format = 'graphml') writes exactly this file for Cytoscape.
set.seed(0)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2.2, 0.5))
lay <- layout_with_fr(g, niter = 300)
plot(g, layout = lay, vertex.size = ifelse(V(g)$type, 2.2, 1.4),
     vertex.color = ifelse(V(g)$type, PAL[["orange"]], PAL[["blue"]]),
     vertex.frame.color = NA, vertex.label = NA, edge.width = 0.2, edge.color = "#00000012",
     main = "1,081 nodes, 16,047 edges: a hairball")
top_t <- names(sort(tdeg, decreasing = TRUE))[1:12]
sel_c <- head(compounds[sapply(compounds, function(c_) sum(Ad[match(c_, compounds), match(top_t, targets)]) >= 6)], 60)
S <- induced_subgraph(g, c(top_t, sel_c))
pos <- rbind(cbind(0, seq_along(top_t)),
             cbind(1, seq_along(sel_c) * length(top_t) / max(1, length(sel_c))))
rownames(pos) <- c(top_t, sel_c); pos <- pos[V(S)$name, ]
plot(S, layout = pos, rescale = FALSE, xlim = c(-1.05, 1.03), ylim = c(0.5, 12.5), asp = 0,
     vertex.size = ifelse(V(S)$name %in% top_t, 7, 2.5),
     vertex.color = ifelse(V(S)$name %in% top_t, PAL[["orange"]], PAL[["blue"]]),
     vertex.frame.color = NA,
     vertex.label = ifelse(V(S)$name %in% top_t, tname[V(S)$name], NA),
     vertex.label.cex = 0.38, vertex.label.dist = 3.4, vertex.label.degree = pi,
     vertex.label.color = "black", edge.width = 0.3, edge.color = "#00000040",
     main = sprintf("12 busiest targets, %d profiled compounds", length(sel_c)))

Figure 8. The same data drawn twice. Left: all 1,081 nodes in a Fruchterman-Reingold layout; dense, unlabelled and dominated by layout artefacts. Right: the twelve busiest targets (orange, labelled) with the compounds profiled against at least six of them (blue), drawn as a bipartite layout — here a reader can see that almost every broadly profiled compound touches both ROCK kinases and most of the tyrosine kinases, which is the sentence this section needs. The left panel belongs in no paper; the right panel is a figure.

Exercise 3

Open the exported backbone.graphml in Cytoscape, colour the nodes by the community attribute and size them by backbone_degree. Then write the two-sentence caption you would use if the figure had to show all 437 backbone targets instead of twelve — and explain why the table of community sizes and kinase fractions from section 4 serves the reader better.

10. Summary

This unit analysed a measured drug-target network: 602 compounds, 479 human single-protein targets, 16,047 activity edges, one connected component, density 0.0275. Ninety-three per cent of the compounds bind more than one target — real polypharmacology, with a median compound degree of 5 and a maximum of 386, and a median target degree of 26 against ROCK1’s 344. Before any interpretation, two selection biases were measured rather than asserted: 79 % of the targets are named “kinase” and carry 83 % of the edges, so the graph is a ROCK-kinase neighbourhood and not a sample of pharmacological space; and the rank correlation between a compound’s degree and the number of measurements behind its edges is 0.93, so degree records assay effort at least as much as promiscuity. ChEMBL’s protein-class annotation was empty for all 479 targets, an annotation gap worked around with target names rather than hidden.

The target projection has 100,146 edges and density 0.875 untreated — no usable structure — and was reduced to a backbone of 12,810 edges at Jaccard 0.3, leaving 42 targets isolated. Greedy modularity found 17 communities at Q = 0.304 (Louvain, 13 at Q = 0.325), the two largest holding 179 and 177 targets of which 91 % and 79 % are named “kinase”, plus a small non-kinase community dominated by carbonic anhydrases and a four-member cytochrome P450 community — the counter-screens and ADME panels of a kinase programme. A bipartite degree-preserving null, written explicitly so that swaps exchange target endpoints, showed why both numbers need a null: the mean Jaccard over target pairs is 0.1482 observed against 0.1424 +/- 0.0003 randomised (z = 17, a 4 % effect), while the backbone holds 12,810 edges against 2,079 +/- 122 (z = 88, a six-fold excess). Structure lives in the tail, not the average. Centrality told the same story about provenance: exact betweenness is led by ROCK1 (0.314) and ROCK2 (0.096) and then by the most-assayed compounds, and correlates with degree at Spearman 0.86.

The selectivity question was answered directly from the 276 compounds measured at both ROCK isoforms: potencies correlate at r = 0.870 (Spearman 0.851), the mean difference is -0.50 log units in favour of ROCK2, 15.6 % of compounds exceed tenfold selectivity and the extreme is -3.55; 68 compounds are measured at ROCK1 only and 34 at ROCK2 only, so a missing edge is a missing experiment and not an inactivity. The panel-wide version of the same question — the gap between the best and tenth-best potency of the 174 compounds profiled at twenty targets or more — has a median of 1.47 log units and falls with the number of targets measured (Spearman -0.379). Link prediction gave the sharpest methodological result: three-step path counting reaches ROC-AUC 0.927 against uniformly drawn negatives — but so does preferential attachment at 0.921, which is the warning — and against negatives matched on target degree the three baselines fall to 0.561, 0.586 and 0.506. Finally, comparing the two kinds of edge showed that chemical similarity implies shared targets (pairs above Tanimoto 0.6 share 83 % of their targets against a 16 % baseline) while the converse fails (overall Spearman 0.28), so a similarity network is a high-precision, low-recall proxy for a measured one.

The three habits to keep: state how every edge was defined and with which threshold; compare every network statistic with a degree-preserving null before interpreting it; and choose the negatives of a graph benchmark as carefully as the decoys of a screening benchmark. A real project adds the graphs this unit did not download — STRING[7] for protein interactions, Open Targets[20] for target-disease evidence, Hetionet[6] for a knowledge graph — and applies the same machinery[22][23][24], including the small-world and network-medicine framings[11][25].

11. Self-assessment

  1. Your bipartite projection has density 0.875. What went wrong, and what do you do?

Nothing went wrong - projections of dense bipartite graphs are nearly complete, because almost every pair of targets shares at least one compound. Threshold the projection into a backbone (here Jaccard 0.3, which keeps 12,810 of 100,146 edges), report the threshold, and check how many nodes it isolates (42 here).

  1. Why is the Jaccard coefficient preferable to the raw count of shared compounds as a projection weight?

Because the raw count grows with the degrees: ROCK1 shares many compounds with everything simply because 344 compounds were measured against it. The Jaccard coefficient divides by the union, so a pair of small, highly overlapping target sets can outrank a pair of large, weakly overlapping ones.

  1. The mean Jaccard is 4 % above its degree-preserving null but the backbone has six times more edges than the null. Which do you report?

Both, and the explanation: the average is almost fixed by the degree sequence, while the excess is concentrated in the upper tail. A statistic with a tail (number of strong links, modularity, a specific pair’s overlap) is the one worth testing; an average that a null reproduces to within 4 % carries almost no information.

  1. Why must a degree-preserving swap in a bipartite graph exchange endpoints on the same side?

Because swapping across sides would create compound-compound or target-target edges and destroy the bipartite structure, changing the object rather than randomising it. The swap used here takes two compound-target edges and exchanges their targets, which preserves every degree on both sides.

  1. A compound has no edge to ROCK2. Is it ROCK1-selective?

No conclusion is possible. The absence of an edge means no measurement with a pChEMBL value exists in this extraction - 68 compounds here are measured at ROCK1 and not at ROCK2. Selectivity requires both measurements; the 276 compounds that have them are the only ones about which the question can be asked.

  1. Your link-prediction model reaches ROC-AUC 0.93. What is the first thing to check?

How the negatives were drawn, and what a degree-only baseline scores. Here preferential attachment - the product of the two degrees, which knows nothing about structure - reached 0.921 against uniform negatives, and against degree-matched negatives every method collapsed to 0.51-0.59. A benchmark is as hard as its negatives.

  1. In a bipartite graph the usual common-neighbour score is always zero. Why, and what replaces it?

A compound and a target are on opposite sides, so they have no neighbours in common; the shortest informative path has length three. The bipartite analogues count three-step paths (compound - target - compound - target), or weight them by the similarity of the two compounds’ target profiles.

  1. Degree correlates with the number of measurements at Spearman 0.93. What does that do to a “most promiscuous compounds” list?

It makes it mostly a list of the most thoroughly profiled compounds. To rank promiscuity one must condition on assay effort - for instance by restricting to compounds screened in a common panel, or by modelling the hit rate (targets hit divided by targets tested) rather than the raw degree. The panel-wide selectivity index of section 6 is one such conditioning, and it still correlates with effort at -0.38.

  1. Your communities are 91 % kinases. Is that biology?

It is provenance. The compounds were selected as ROCK1 ligands and were therefore assayed mainly in kinase panels, so the graph can hardly contain anything else; 79 % of all targets in it are named “kinase”. The community structure faithfully describes the data set and says nothing about pharmacological space in general.

  1. Greedy modularity returns 17 communities at Q = 0.304 and Louvain returns 13 at Q = 0.325 on the same backbone. Which is correct?

Neither is “the” answer: both are heuristics for the same NP-hard objective, and a higher Q simply means a better optimum was found. Report the algorithm, its parameters and the modularity, and check that the conclusion you draw (here, that the communities are kinase panels) survives both partitions. The resolution limit means that neither can reliably detect families smaller than a few nodes.

  1. ChEMBL returned no protein class for any target. How should the analysis report that?

Explicitly: state the coverage (0 of 479 here), use a declared surrogate - a text match on the target name in this unit - and label every class-based statement as derived from that surrogate. Silently dropping the annotation, or quietly substituting another source without saying so, is what makes an analysis unreproducible.

  1. What minimum information must accompany any network result?

The node and edge definitions, every threshold used, the number of nodes and edges, the provenance and selection rule of the data, the software and version, the null model with the number of randomisations, and - for link prediction - how the negatives were sampled.

Glossary

Bipartite graph
A graph whose nodes split into two sets with edges only between the sets, such as compounds and targets; marked in igraph by the logical vertex attribute type.
Projection
Graph on one side of a bipartite network, joining two nodes that share a neighbour; weighted by shared counts or by a Jaccard coefficient.
Backbone
The subgraph left after discarding projection edges below a weight threshold; a projection is uninterpretable without one.
Degree
Number of edges at a node; here the number of targets a compound was measured at, or compounds a target was screened with.
pChEMBL
-log10 of the molar concentration of a measured activity (IC50, Ki, Kd); 7 means 100 nM, and one unit is a factor of ten.
Polypharmacology / selectivity
Binding several targets / preferring one target over its relatives; a tenfold preference is one pChEMBL unit.
Betweenness centrality
Fraction of shortest paths passing through a node; in a designed data set it reproduces the design before it reveals biology.
Eigenvector centrality
Importance defined recursively by the importance of neighbours; well defined only on a connected graph, and scaled by igraph so that the maximum is 1.
Bipartite clustering coefficient
Mean neighbourhood overlap (here the Jaccard “dot” mode) between a node and the nodes two hops away; the bipartite replacement for a triangle count.
Modularity Q
Fraction of edges inside communities minus the fraction expected in a degree-preserving random graph.
Resolution limit
Inability of modularity maximisation to detect communities below a size that grows with the graph.
Degree-preserving randomisation
Rewiring that keeps every node’s degree and destroys everything else; in a bipartite graph the swap must exchange endpoints on the same side.
Link prediction
Scoring absent edges by plausibility; bipartite baselines count three-step paths, weight them by profile similarity, or multiply degrees.
Hard negatives
Non-edges chosen to be plausible - here matched on target degree - rather than uniformly at random.
Assay-effort bias
Degree reflecting how much a node has been measured rather than its biology; here Spearman 0.93 between compound degree and number of measurements.
Annotation gap
A metadata field that is absent for part or all of the data (here protein class for 479 of 479 targets), to be reported and worked around explicitly.
